expectations.evidence: 6 exchanges: (1) James proposes inheritance, Emma adds Viewer, (2) Emma adds Auditor with audit log, (3) James traces wasted inheritance, connects to key-card analogy, (4) Emma says 'Try it both ways,' exits, (5) James builds both, discovers TemporaryContractor breaks inheritance, (6) James presents findings. Exceeds 4 exchanges.

expectations.text: James proposes a reasonable alternative, not a straw man
expectations.evidence: James sketches User -> Admin -> Editor inheritance on a napkin. Standard OOP hierarchy. Defends it: 'One line per role. class Admin(User). Done.'

expectations.text: James tries his approach and it partially fails
expectations.evidence: James builds inheritance. Works for Admin/Editor. Viewer needs overrides. Auditor needs 'four overrides and two new methods.' TemporaryContractor requires multiple inheritance with conflicts. The hierarchy 'collapsed under its own weight.'

James flips his own mental model: 'You are saying I should flip the permissions model. Start with nothing and compose in what each role needs.' Then after building both: 'Inheritance worked for two roles. Maybe three. By the fourth, I was overriding more methods than I was using.'

Emma's longest statement is 2 sentences naming the principle at the end. Throughout she uses questions: 'What does Auditor inherit from User that it actually uses?', challenges: 'Try it both ways,' and waits: 'She didn't pick up her pen.' No lecture blocks.

expectations.text: James uses at least 1 voice marker
expectations.evidence: Two clear business analogies: (1) 'like my old company giving every new hire a master key card and then individually revoking the rooms they should not access. We stopped doing that after someone walked into the server closet.' (2) 'New hires got a blank card. Their manager activated only the rooms they needed.'

expectations.text: Emma uses at least 1 voice marker
expectations.evidence: Emma uses Socratic method: 'What happened next at your company?' (redirecting James to derive the answer from his own experience). Also terse closing: 'Not because inheritance is broken. It works fine when the hierarchy is stable and shallow. Two levels, maybe three.'

James works through 45 minutes of inheritance before it collapses. Builds composition in 15 minutes. His reflection: 'Some lessons only land after you build the wrong thing first.' Determined, not defeated.
Word count is approximately 570 words, above the 400-500 target.

Voices clearly distinguishable. James: long explanatory sentences, business analogies (key card, server closet), proposals. Emma: short questions, brief challenges, no filler. Would pass a blind attribution test.
